It’s great that you’re thinking about how the letter reads—tone matters a lot in patient communications. However, automatically using “she” for a nurse can be a problem because it relies on an old stereotype that all nurses are women, which isn’t accurate. Men and non-binary people are nurses too, and using “she” as the default can make those colleagues invisible and feel exclusionary to patients and staff.

Instead, you can keep the letter natural and inclusive with a few simple options:

- **Use the singular “they”:** “Your nurse will introduce themselves and they will check your vitals.” This is grammatically correct and widely accepted.
- **Rewrite to avoid the pronoun entirely:** “Your nurse will greet you and check your vitals.” Or, if you need to refer back: “The nurse will review your history; this team member will also answer any questions.”
- **Use the nurse’s name or title if you’re referring to a specific person:** “Nurse Alex will be with you shortly. Alex will help you get settled.”

If the letter is about a particular nurse whose pronouns you know are she/her, feel free to use “she.” But for a welcome letter that might apply to any nurse on your team, switching to gender-neutral language makes it welcoming for everyone—patients and staff alike—without losing a natural flow.

I hear you—it’s not a myth that nursing is a predominantly female profession. In the U.S., for example, around 87–90% of nurses are women, so your personal experience makes perfect sense and is shared by a lot of people.

The issue isn’t whether “most nurses are women” is true. It’s that a welcome letter like this isn’t describing a statistic—it’s **talking about an individual** who could be any nurse on your team. When you use “she” as the default pronoun, you’re not just noting a pattern; you’re making an assumption about a specific person before they’ve walked into the room. That’s where it can feel exclusionary, even if unintentionally.

A few things to consider:

- **For the male and non-binary nurses on your staff**, seeing “she” used for their role in an official patient communication can make them feel invisible, like they don’t quite belong in the picture the practice is painting.
- **For patients**, it subtly reinforces the idea that a male nurse is somehow a deviation from the norm, which can lead to awkward “oh, you’re a nurse?” moments that many men in nursing report experiencing regularly.
- **It’s not about ignoring reality, but about avoiding unnecessary assumptions when writing hypothetically.** When we refer to a hypothetical doctor as "they" now (even though doctors were historically often "he" in writing), it's the same principle—the facts of the field's demographics don't have to dictate the pronouns we use for the role in general communication.

You absolutely can write naturally without “she.” A line like “Your nurse will walk you to the room and check your vitals” is clean, friendly, and doesn’t trip up on gender. If you really want to use a pronoun, singular “they” (“they will help you”) reads completely smoothly to most people’s ears today.

So to your original question—“Does that work?”—I’d say it works in the sense that it’s readable, but it doesn’t work for making every patient and staff member feel fully welcomed. And a welcome letter is one place where that’s worth getting right.

You're right that it was just normal for a long time — the same way we’d say “he” for a doctor, a fireman, or a soldier. And you're also right that it reflected what people saw every day. So it's not that you're imagining things or that it was secretly a huge problem nobody talked about until now.

The shift isn't really about denying reality; it's about what we now understand that *language does* when we make those assumptions. A few things changed:

- **We became more aware of who was being left out.** Male nurses have always existed (they made up a much larger share before the 1900s, actually), but using “she” as the blanket pronoun makes them invisible. When you're part of a group that's constantly assumed not to exist in your job, it wears on you. Early male nurses and female doctors spoke up more over time, and we started listening.
- **We started seeing the same problem across the board.** It wasn't just nurses. People pushed back against “he” for doctors, “fireman,” “policeman,” “chairman.” The shift to “firefighter,” “police officer,” “server” instead of “waitress,” etc., came from the same realization: using the statistical majority as the *default word for the human in the role* made the minority feel like exceptions who didn't quite belong.
- **Welcoming people became the goal in settings like yours.** A welcome letter isn't a sociology report about who *usually* does the job. It's speaking to a patient about the human who will walk into the room. If that human happens to be a man, starting the letter with “she” makes your practice look like it didn't even consider the possibility. That can make the nurse feel like a surprise rather than a professional, and it can make the patient react awkwardly.

So it’s less “suddenly everything is a problem” and more “we now have the language tools and the awareness to do better without much effort.” A simple “they” or just avoiding the pronoun fixes it. And if it still reads naturally—which it does in “Your nurse will take you to the exam room and check your vitals”—then there's really no downside.

You don't have to throw away the reality that nursing is mostly women. That's still true. It's just that, in a welcome letter meant to make *everyone* feel comfortable—patients and staff alike—a small adjustment goes a long way.
